title: Building Block Three: The Job No Leader Should Delegate
hook: Fresh toner on a promotion packet cannot cover what the floor already knows about fit.
counterintuition: The kind move can protect a misfit role and still be the harsh one when the team pays for the leader's comfort.
tryThisNow: Choose one role that feels avoided. Write the current demand of the role, the person's real behavior, and the next honest action.
keyTakeaway: The right people in the right jobs require leaders to choose role truth over comfort, loyalty, and vague admiration.

breakdown.fastRead:
Beck lifts a promotion packet from the copier while the pick line waits for a supervisor nobody trusts. The packet praises loyalty. The floor is paying for poor fit.

Own the people call as execution work. First name what the role now needs. Then compare that demand with what you have seen. If the gap is real, choose coaching, a new seat, or a harder action before delay becomes the system. A warm tie cannot carry a job built for a different kind of judgment.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 6:58 p.m., Lirit reads a nurse manager file in a stairwell while two charge nurses argue over missed medication checks. The candidate is admired, but the role now requires fast conflict decisions and she has avoided three of them.

You can see the mechanism in the first awkward pause. People tend to protect a promise after it has been spoken out loud. They smooth bad news, widen dates, and call vague ownership teamwork. Owning people placement with courage, knowledge, and clear fit judgment cuts through that comfort by asking for the live fact that changes action.

At 2:49 p.m., Nestor watches a beloved plant lead charm a customer tour while his maintenance backlog grows behind the curtain. The useful move is not louder pressure. It is closer contact with the work. Ask who owns the next hard move, what might block it, and what proof will be visible soon. Then stay long enough to change the plan when the answer is rough.

At 8:24 a.m., Coralie realizes courage is not cruelty when a misfit role has been draining four stronger people for months. There is a limit. Strong execution cannot make a weak premise true. It can only expose the weak premise early, while a leader still has time to change the promise, move the person, narrow the goal, or stop pretending.
breakdown.fullRead:
Beck stops beside the copier with the promotion packet still warm from the machine. The candidate is liked, loyal, and easy to defend. On the floor, three supervisors already know the truth the packet avoids: the role now requires tough compliance decisions, and this person has spent a year stepping around them.

Getting the right people in the right jobs is execution work because every role carries a piece of the plan. Put the wrong person there and the cost spreads. Other people compensate. Decisions wait. Standards soften. The strategy looks intact while the role that should carry it becomes a bottleneck.

The causes are rarely mysterious. Sometimes leaders lack direct knowledge. They know the reputation, not the behavior. Sometimes they lack courage. They can describe the mismatch privately but will not act on it. Often the psychological comfort factor is strongest of all: the easy relationship, the old loyalty, the relief of not having a hard conversation today.

The better question is not whether the person is good. It is whether the person fits the work the business now needs. Does the role require someone who energizes people through a hard change? Someone decisive on tough issues? Someone who gets things done through others instead of carrying everything alone? Someone who follows through when the first answer is uncomfortable?

At the hospital-wing project, Mathieu keeps looking at the superintendent's name because he wants the relationship to stay simple. The punch list says otherwise. The subcontractor sequence is too tight, the inspection date is fixed, and friendliness will not coordinate the job. Naming that fact is not cruelty. It is commitment to the work and to the people currently paying for the mismatch.

There is a humane way to do this badly and a humane way to do it well. Badly means hiding behind labels, making the person the problem, or pretending one conversation solves every fit issue. Well means stating the role demand, the observed behavior, the cost of the gap, and the next action without contempt.

The unvarnished truth is not a license to be harsh. It is a refusal to let comfort keep damaging the role, the team, and the result.

A leader cannot delegate the courage to see fit clearly.

Comfort has a cost ledger of its own. It appears as extra supervision, quiet rework, missed handoffs, and talented people learning that truth is less welcome than loyalty. The leader who postpones the fit decision is still making a decision. The team pays for it while the conversation is being avoided.

This is why the work cannot be handed off as a personnel chore. Human resources can support the process, gather facts, and protect fairness. The leader still owns the judgment about what the role requires and whether the person in it can carry that requirement now. If that judgment is outsourced, execution gets outsourced with it.

examples.title: Beck stops the promotion packet at the copier

planSpec.domain: an operations leader reviewing a promotion packet for a weak floor supervisor
planSpec.audience: a leader tempted to accept a comfortable promotion recommendation
planSpec.stakes: a pick line that will inherit the cost of a poor fit
planSpec.requiredBeat: he smells fresh toner on the packet and faces the fit truth the floor already knows

examples.scenario: At 10:36 a.m., Beck lifts the promotion packet from the copier while the toner is still warm. The recommendation says Turlough is ready for pick-line supervisor. Ten feet away, packers are waiting for a slotting call Turlough has avoided since dawn. He is liked, punctual, and careful with reports. He also freezes when two leads disagree. Beck's pen is above the approval box. He must decide whether pleasant history is enough for a job that now needs fast calls.
examples.whatToDo: Hold the promotion, write the role demands in plain language, and meet Turlough with a development path tied to real supervisor decisions.
examples.whyItMatters: Fit is about the work now, not affection or tenure. A comfortable promotion can move the cost onto everyone the supervisor must lead.

examples.title: Lirit reads the nurse manager file in the stairwell

planSpec.domain: a nursing director deciding whether a liked candidate can handle conflict-heavy manager work
planSpec.audience: a director balancing loyalty with patient safety
planSpec.stakes: missed medication checks and a unit that needs decisive leadership
planSpec.requiredBeat: she names the conflict gap instead of approving the liked candidate

examples.scenario: "Everyone trusts Calla," the clinic director says while Lirit grips the nurse manager file in the north stairwell. "Everyone trusts Calla," the recruiter says through the phone. On the landing below, two charge nurses are still arguing about missed medication checks. Lirit says, "Trust is not the whole job." The recruiter goes quiet. The file smells like printer ink. Lirit must decide whether to say the harder part: Calla has avoided every conflict this unit now needs her to face.
examples.whatToDo: Name the conflict requirement, pause the appointment, and test Calla against that requirement with a clear coaching plan or a different role.
examples.whyItMatters: Courage protects both the person and the work. Avoiding the fit truth lets a liked candidate fail in public later.

examples.title: Nestor watches charm hide the maintenance backlog

planSpec.domain: a plant leader judging a charismatic lead whose follow-through is weak
planSpec.audience: a leader who confuses customer charm with execution strength
planSpec.stakes: a maintenance backlog that can shut down a line
planSpec.requiredBeat: he must decide whether the charming tour changes the fit problem

examples.scenario: The visitors laugh at Vale's safety-glasses joke while Nestor watches the maintenance board behind the curtain. The visitors laugh, and Nestor has to decide whether charm is hiding the role-fit failure. Behind the curtain, the maintenance board has fourteen overdue red tags, seven with Vale's initials beside first review. Nestor has been telling himself Vale energizes people. The customer lead asks if Vale is the permanent operations head. Nestor smiles, then sees the red tags through the window.
examples.whatToDo: Separate charm from execution. Review Vale against follow-through, hard calls, and backlog ownership before making any role promise.
examples.whyItMatters: A person can energize a room and still fail the job. Placement judgment has to match role demand, not the easiest visible strength.

examples.title: Coralie counts the four people carrying one misfit role

planSpec.domain: a retail district manager reviewing the hidden load caused by a poor store-manager fit
planSpec.audience: a leader who delayed a staffing decision in the name of patience
planSpec.stakes: burnout among stronger employees and a store that never stabilizes
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees the cost of delay spread across four other people

examples.scenario: It takes four printed resignation texts on Coralie's passenger seat to show who is carrying one misfit role. Each one mentions helping the manager catch up after close. She had called it patience. She had called it giving Huw time. Now she circles the same phrase in all four notes: doing his job too. The mall doors are still locked. Coralie writes the sentence she avoided for three months: this role is bigger than Huw can carry today.
examples.whatToDo: Stop calling the delay development. Reassign the role, give Huw a smaller path he can win, and repair the load carried by the remaining team.
examples.whyItMatters: Avoidance has a payroll. When one person is badly placed, stronger people quietly subsidize the decision until they leave.

examples.title: Rikke opens the succession folder after the fire drill

planSpec.domain: a logistics executive discovering a succession plan is only one name deep
planSpec.audience: a leader who mistook a favorite backup for real depth
planSpec.stakes: operational continuity after a warehouse emergency
planSpec.requiredBeat: a fire drill exposes that the bench is not real

examples.scenario: What does a sealed succession folder prove after a fire drill leaves thirty drivers waiting in the yard? Before the drill, the folder looked complete because one respected dispatcher was listed under site lead backup. After the drill, everyone learned he was on vacation and no second person knew the hazmat gate call tree. Rikke writes two columns on the folder flap: named backup and tested backup. Only one column has ink.
examples.whatToDo: Build real depth by naming and testing second backups for critical roles, not just storing a favorite name in a folder.
examples.whyItMatters: Succession depth is proved under absence. One admired backup is a hope, not a process that can carry the work.

examples.title: Tavon hears himself call avoidance patience

planSpec.domain: a nonprofit director realizing he is avoiding a staff fit conversation
planSpec.audience: a mission-driven leader who dislikes hard personnel judgment
planSpec.stakes: program quality and a coordinator who may need a different role
planSpec.requiredBeat: he catches the comforting word he has used to delay a clear fit call

examples.scenario: You sit with Tavon in the after-school center while bead bins stay open and tomorrow's volunteer schedule is half filled. He hears himself tell the board chair, again, that Rowena needs more time as program coordinator. The phrase sounds kind until he looks at the parent complaints clipped under a magnet. Three late pickups, two missing allergy forms, one locked supply closet. Patience is not the word anymore. His mouth is dry when he picks up the phone.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the vague promise of more time with a fit conversation: current role demands, observed misses, and the next role or support decision.
examples.whyItMatters: Clear judgment is not the enemy of care. It is what lets care become a role that the person and the program can actually carry.

reviewCards.front: A plan sounds clear, but the next hard owner is unnamed. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the execution test: name the owner, the next action, the date, and the evidence that will prove the work moved.

reviewCards.front: A team gives calm status while field evidence feels rough. What move keeps truth close?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the raw signal from the place where the work happens, then decide what changes before the next review.

reviewCards.front: You spot a comforting story covering a weak handoff. What question breaks the spell?
reviewCards.back: Ask what must be true by a near date, who owns that proof, and what will happen if the proof does not appear.

reviewCards.front: A target was built on a false assumption. What does strong follow-through require?
reviewCards.back: Change the target, name the failed premise, and protect the system from pretending the old promise still fits reality.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: owning people placement with courage, knowledge, and clear fit judgment starts with a live promise and forces it into owned action. The habit is to ask what is true now, who owns the next hard move, and what proof will appear soon.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work plan earns quick agreement, then I will ask for the owner, date, and proof point on the hardest piece before I call it ready.
If I set a health goal, then I will name the next physical setup, the time it happens, and the check I will use tomorrow.
If I keep repeating a personal promise, then I will turn it into one visible action with a time, place, and fallback.
If someone depends on me, then I will state exactly what I will do next and when they can see or hear the result.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, choose one promise that sounds settled and write the owner, the next action, the riskiest assumption, and the proof you expect to see within seven days.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, end each serious planning conversation by asking what changed, who owns the next hard move, and what evidence will be visible before the next check-in.
